Judgment :

1. Vide this award cum judgment, I shall dispose of a claim petition filed under Section 140 & 166 of Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 (hereinafter referred to as "M.V. Act") by the claimants being the LRs of deceased claiming compensation for the untimely death of the deceased Jagvir Singh in an accident which took place on 26.10.2019 at around 10.00 AM, due to the rash and negligent act of driver of the offending vehicle bearing no. DL-9CH-2951.
2.
The brief facts as per present petition are that on 26.10.2019 at about 10.00 AM the deceased was going to his Village Basoli from Gonda after taking household items from market.
When he reached in front of Kanya Inter College Gate, Gonda then suddenly a car bearing no. DL-9CH-2951 came and hit the deceased from back side.
Due to said impact, the deceased suffered grievous injuries and subsequently died on 30.10.2019 during his treatment.
3. Notice of the petition were sent to the respondents.

However, despite service, the driver and owner have not appeared and were proceeded ex-parte vide order dated Anshul Verma and ors. vs.
National Insurance Company Ltd. and ors.
26.07.2022 passed by my Ld. Predecessor.

However, it is admitted that the offending vehicle bearing No. DL-9CH-2951 was insured with respondent No.1 vide policy No.
461700311810008696 in the name of Firoz Akhtar for the period from 06.02.2019 to 05.02.2020.

4. From the pleadings of the parties, following issues were framed vide order dated 26.07.2022 by my Ld. Predecessor :-
1.

Whether Jagvir Singh received fatal injuries in a road accident on 26.10.2019 infront of Kanya Inter College Gate, Gonda, due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle bearing no.
DL-9CH-2951 being driven by respondent no. 3 (driver), owned by respondent no. 2 (owner) and insured with respondent no. 1(National Insurance Company Ltd)?

(OPP) 
2. To what amount of compensation the LRs of the deceased are entitled and from whom?
3. Relief.

sentences.text:
The said accident occurred due to negligence of vehicle bearing no.
DL-9CH-2951 as the said vehicle hit the vehicle and deceased from behind.
In his cross-examination by Ld. counsel for the insurance company, he stated that he is the eye witness to the accident.
He had gone to get his vehicle repaired and he was standing at a distance of 10 feet away from the place of accident.
The deceased was standing alongside the road along with his motorcycle.
The deceased was talking on phone.
The road was single road and there is no divider on the road.
He denied the suggestion that due to his own negligence, deceased died in the accident.
The driver of the offending vehicle fled from the spot after hitting the deceased.
He further stated in his cross-examination that he had noted down the registration number of the offending vehicle immediately in his mind and later on he noted it on the paper.
He had not taken the deceased to the hospital.
He called the police and police had reached the spot within twenty - thirty minutes after the accident.
He denied the suggestion that he has come to depose before the court in order to help the victims in getting the compensation.

Counsel for the petitioners argued forcefully that from the evidence led coupled with the criminal record placed, the petitioners have proved the fact that it was the driver of the offending vehicle who was responsible for causing fatal injuries to the deceased Jagvir Singh by his rash and negligent driving.

sentences.text: Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the respondent no. 1/ insurance company stated that present petition is not maintainable as FIR was lodged after five days from the date of accident and even then he could not mention the registration number.
The deceased was himself negligent.
Therefore, the insurance company is not liable to pay compensation.
11. It is a settled legal position that while deciding a petition u/s 166 of the M V Act, the Claims Tribunal has to decide negligence on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.

Reference in this regard is made to the observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Kaushnumma Begum and Others v/s New India Assurance Company Limited, 2001 ACJ 421 SC, wherein it was held that the issue of wrongful act or omission on the part of the driver of motor vehicle involved in the accident is of secondary importance and mere use or involvement of motor vehicle in causing bodily injuries or death to a human being or damage to property would make the petition maintainable u/s 166 & 140 of the M V Act.

16. As far as delay in registration of FIR is concerned, it is a lapse on the part of the police official.

Otherwise also, lodging of F.I.R. certainly proves the factum of the accident so that the victim can file a compensation case, but delay in doing so cannot be the sole ground for rejecting the claim petition.
Even the wife of the deceased in her cross-examination has specifically submitted that her husband was hospitalised for five days after the accident.
In the circumstances of the case, the same can be treated as a proper explanation for the delay in lodging of the FIR.

17. In the present case, it is pertinent to note that the respondent no. 3/ driver of the aforesaid vehicle bearing no. DL- 9CH-2951 was the material witness to throw light by testifying as to how and under what circumstances, the accident had taken place.

18. Hitting from behind per-se amounts to negligence unless explained otherwise.
Even the charge sheet has been filed against the respondent no.3.
No other version of accident is explained or proved on record except the one narrated by the injured.
19. On the basis of evidence on record, above observation and discussion it is proved that the abovesaid accident took place due to rash and negligent driving of R3 Bal Krishan Upadhyay.

Accordingly, issue no. 1 is decided in favour of the petitioners.
ISSUE NO.2 20.
As the offending vehicle was being driven by respondent no.3/ Bal Krishan Upadhyay, therefore primary liability to compensate the petitioner is that of respondent no.3.
As the offending vehicle was owned by respondent no.2/ Firoz Akhtar, therefore, he becomes vicariously liable to compensate the petitioner.
The offending vehicle was insured with respondent no.1/ Insurance Company, therefore, respondent no.1/ Insurance Company becomes contractually liable to pay the compensation to the petitioners.

Act") by the claimants being the LRs of deceased claiming compensation for the untimely death of the deceased Jagvir Singh in an accident which took place on 26.10.2019 at around 10.00 AM, due to the rash and negligent act of driver of the offending vehicle bearing no. DL-9CH-2951.
2.
Due to said impact, the deceased suffered grievous injuries and subsequently died on 30.10.2019 during his treatment.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
Anshul Verma and ors. vs. National Insurance Company Ltd. and ors.
12.
The deceased was himself negligent.
Therefore, the insurance company is not liable to pay compensation.
11. It is a settled legal position that while deciding a petition u/s 166 of the M V Act, the Claims Tribunal has to decide negligence on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:

4 12.
Nevertheless, it is also a settled legal position that in a claim petition u/s 166 of the M V Act,
burden is on the claimants/petitioners to prove negligence.
The law to this effect declared in Minu B Mehta Vs. Balkrishna Ramchandra Nayan (1977) 2 SC 441 was reiterated by the Supreme Court in Oriental Anshul Verma and ors. vs. National Insurance Company Ltd. and ors.
Insurance Company Limited vs. Meena Variyal 2007 (5) SCC 428, which has been followed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in a recent case, New India Assurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Devki & Ors., MAC APP 165/2013 decided on 29.02.2016.
13. Certified copies of criminal proceedings filed alongwith it are admissible in evidence and deemed to be correct under Rule 7 of the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal Rules, 2008 until proved to be contrary.
14. In this regard observations made by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in New India Assurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana and Ors. reported in 2007 SCC online DEL 1700 has to be considered wherein it was held that :-
"the wife of the deceased had produced (1) certified copy of criminal record of criminal case in FIR No. 955/2004 pertaining to involvement of the offending vehicle; (2) Criminal record showing completion of investigation of police and issue of charage-sheet under Section 279/304-A IPC against the driver; (3) certified copy of FIR wherein criminal case against the drive was lodged; and (4 ) recover memo and mechanical inspection report of the offending vehicle and vehicle of the deceased.
15. In the present case also, copies of criminal proceedings which have been filed alongwith the petition, have not been challenged and controverted by any of the respondents.
Police Anshul Verma and ors. vs. National Insurance Company Ltd. and ors.
after investigation had filed charge-sheet against the respondents which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent no. 3/driver in causing the accident.
16. As far as delay in registration of FIR is concerned, it is a lapse on the part of the police official.
Otherwise also, lodging of F.I.R. certainly proves the factum of the accident so that the victim can file a compensation case, but delay in doing so cannot be the sole ground for rejecting the claim petition.
Even the wife of the deceased in her cross-examination has specifically submitted that her husband was hospitalised for five days after the accident.
In the circumstances of the case, the same can be treated as a proper explanation for the delay in lodging of the FIR.
17. In the present case, it is pertinent to note that the respondent no. 3/ driver of the aforesaid vehicle bearing no. DL- 9CH-2951 was the material witness to throw light by testifying as to how and under what circumstances, the accident had taken place.
However, he has preferred not to enter into Anshul Verma And Ors vs National Insurance Co. And Ors on 17 October, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107005442/

Thus, an adverse inference is liable to be drawn against him to the effect that the accident in question occurred due to rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle.
The driver did not enter into the witness box to controvert the claim of the petitioners or even to explain the Anshul Verma and ors. vs. National Insurance Company Ltd. and ors.
circumstances of accident.
As the offending vehicle was being driven by respondent no.3/ Bal Krishan Upadhyay, therefore primary liability to compensate the petitioner is that of respondent no.3.
As the offending vehicle was owned by respondent no.2/ Firoz Akhtar, therefore, he becomes vicariously liable to compensate the petitioner.
The offending vehicle was insured with respondent no.1/ Insurance Company, therefore, respondent no.1/ Insurance Company becomes contractually liable to pay the compensation to the petitioners.

I am satisfied that his income should be taken as Rs.60,838/- per month for calculating his dependency.
After adding future prospects, the income of the deceased comes to Rs.79,089/-
(Rs.60,838/- + Rs.60,838/-x 30/100).
Admittedly, the deceased was married leaving behind legal heirs i.e. Smt. Anshul Verma (wife of th deceased), Sh. Mayank Pratap Singh (son of the deceased),
Ms. Diksha Rani (daughter of the deceased) and Smt. Phoolwati Devi (mother of the deceased).
Therefore, one fourth is to be deducted towards personal and living expenses of the deceased.
After deduction, the income of the deceased comes to Rs.59,316/-.
Thus, the loss of dependency comes to Rs.99,65,088/- (Rs.59,316 x 12 x 14).
I therefore, award Rs.99,65,088/- to the petitioners towards loss of dependency.
